## Proof

**Claim:** Yes. There exists an $F$-measurable $g:\Omega\to X$ with $g=f$ $P$-a.e.

We prove this in three steps.

### Step 1. A lifting lemma for indicator functions

**Lemma.** For every $A\in F'$ there exists $B\in F$ with $\mathbf{1}_B = \mathbf{1}_A$ $P$-a.e.

*Proof.* By definition of the completion, $A = B\cup N$ where $B\in F$, $N\subseteq M$, $M\in F$, $P(M)=0$. Then $A\triangle B \subseteq M$, so $P(A\triangle B)=0$, i.e. $\mathbf{1}_A=\mathbf{1}_B$ a.e. $\square$

### Step 2. Approximation of $f$ by $F'$-measurable simple functions converging uniformly

Since $X$ is a compact metric space, it is separable. Let $\{x_1,x_2,\dots\}$ be a countable dense subset. For each $n\ge 1$, the open balls $\{B(x_i,1/n)\}_{i\ge 1}$ cover $X$. Define
$$
A_i^{(n)} \;=\; f^{-1}\!\big(B(x_i,1/n)\big)\;\setminus\;\bigcup_{j<i}f^{-1}\!\big(B(x_j,1/n)\big),\qquad i\ge 1.
$$
Each $f^{-1}(B(x_i,1/n))\in F'$ (since $f$ is $F'$-measurable and the balls are Borel), hence each $A_i^{(n)}\in F'$. The $\{A_i^{(n)}\}_{i\ge 1}$ form a countable measurable partition of $\Omega$, and on $A_i^{(n)}$ we have $d(f(\omega),x_i)<1/n$. Set
$$
f_n(\omega) \;=\; \sum_{i\ge 1} x_i\,\mathbf{1}_{A_i^{(n)}}(\omega).
$$
This is an $F'$-measurable simple function and $d(f(\omega),f_n(\omega))<1/n$ for every $\omega$. Thus $f_n\to f$ **uniformly** (hence pointwise) on $\Omega$.

### Step 3. Replacing each $f_n$ by an $F$-measurable $g_n$ equal a.e., and passing to the limit

By the Lemma, for each $A_i^{(n)}\in F'$ pick $B_i^{(n)}\in F$ with $\mathbf{1}_{B_i^{(n)}}=\mathbf{1}_{A_i^{(n)}}$ a.e. Let $N_i^{(n)}\in F$ with $P(N_i^{(n)})=0$ and $\mathbf{1}_{B_i^{(n)}}=\mathbf{1}_{A_i^{(n)}}$ on $(N_i^{(n)})^c$. Define
$$
g_n(\omega)\;=\;\sum_{i\ge 1}x_i\,\mathbf{1}_{B_i^{(n)}}(\omega).
$$
This is $F$-measurable (pointwise limit of partial sums of $F$-measurable simple functions; or directly: it is a countable-valued $F$-measurable function since each level set $\{g_n=x_i\}=B_i^{(n)}\in F$). 

Set $N=\bigcup_{n,i}N_i^{(n)}\in F$; then $P(N)=0$, and on $N^c$ we have $g_n=f_n$ for **every** $n$. Therefore on $N^c$,
$$
g_n(\omega)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{} f(\omega).
$$

Now define
$$
g(\omega)=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}g_n(\omega), & \text{if the limit exists},\\[4pt]
x_1, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$
The set $E=\{\omega:\lim_n g_n(\omega)\text{ exists}\}$ is $F$-measurable (it is $\bigcap_{k}\bigcup_{N}\bigcap_{m,n\ge N}\{d(g_m,g_n)<1/k\}$, all $F$-measurable sets since $g_n$ are $F$-measurable and $d(\cdot,\cdot)$ is continuous). On $E$, $g=\lim g_n$ is $F$-measurable; on $E^c$, $g$ is constant. Hence $g$ is $F$-measurable.

On $N^c\subseteq E$ we have $g=\lim g_n=\lim f_n=f$. Since $P(N)=0$,
$$
g=f\quad P\text{-a.e.}
$$

This completes the proof. $\blacksquare$
